content: 1. Corticosteroids and ACTH can exacerbate electrolyte depletion, particularly hypokalemia, when used concurrently with certain medications. 2. Pressor amines, such as norepinephrine, may exhibit a reduced response when used with these drugs, but this reduction is not significant enough to contraindicate their use. 3. Nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxants, such as tubocurarine, may show increased responsiveness when used in combination with these medications. 4. Lithium should generally not be co-administered with diuretics, as diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium, significantly increasing the risk of lithium toxicity. 5. Before using lithium preparations with Vaserectic, refer to the specific package insert for guidance. 6. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can reduce the diuretic, natriuretic, and antihypertensive effects of loop, potassium-sparing, and thiazide diuretics in some patients. 7. 8. Drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy can impair fetal renal function and increase fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. 9. Oligohydramnios resulting from such drug use can lead to fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformities. 10. Potential neonatal adverse effects include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, and death. 11. If pregnancy is detected, Vaserectic should be discontinued as soon as possible. 12. These adverse outcomes are typically associated with drug use during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. 13. 14. Proper management of maternal hypertension during pregnancy is crucial to optimize outcomes for both the mother and fetus. 15. In rare cases where no alternative therapy is available, the mother should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. 16. Serial ultrasound examinations should be performed to assess the intra-amniotic environment. 17. If oligohydramnios is observed, Vaserectic should be discontinued unless it is deemed life-saving for the mother. 18. Fetal testing may be appropriate depending on the gestational age. 19. Patients and physicians should be aware that oligohydramnios may not become apparent until after irreversible fetal injury has occurred. 20. 21. No teratogenic effects of enalapril were observed in studies involving pregnant rats and rabbits. 22. Doses used in these studies were significantly higher than the maximum recommended human daily dose (MRHDD) when adjusted for body surface area. 23. In mice and rats, enalapril combined with hydrochlorothiazide at high doses caused fetotoxicity, expressed as reduced average fetal weight. 24. No fetotoxicity was observed at lower doses of enalapril-hydrochlorothiazide. 25. ACE inhibitors, when used during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, can cause injury or death to the developing fetus. 26. If pregnancy is detected, Vaserectic should be discontinued immediately. 27. 28. Exchange transfusions or dialysis may be required to reverse hypotension or substitute for impaired renal function. 29. Enalapril, which crosses the placenta, has been removed from neonatal circulation via peritoneal dialysis with some clinical benefit. Theoretical removal via exchange transfusion is possible, though untested. 30. The safety and effectiveness of Vaserectic in pediatric patients have not been established. 31. This drug is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and patients with impaired renal function are at greater risk of toxic reactions. 32. Elderly patients, who are more likely to have reduced renal function, require careful dose selection. 33. Evaluation of hypertensive patients should always include an assessment of renal function. 34. Vaserectic should be promptly discontinued in cases of adverse reactions, and appropriate therapy and monitoring should be provided until symptoms resolve. 35. Periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts should be considered in patients with collagen vascular disease and renal disease. 36. Renal function should be monitored during the initial weeks of therapy in such patients. 37. Single oral doses of enalapril above 1,000 mg/kg in mice and ≥1,775 mg/kg in rats were associated with lethality. 38. The most likely manifestation of enalapril overdose is hypotension, typically treated with intravenous infusion of normal saline. 39. Enalaprilat can be removed from circulation via hemodialysis and has been removed from neonatal circulation via peritoneal dialysis. 40. Lethality was not observed after oral administration of hydrochlorothiazide at doses of 10 g/kg in mice and rats. 41. Common signs of hydrochlorothiazide overdose include electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hyponatremia) and dehydration due to excessive diuresis. 42. If digitalis has also been administered, hypokalemia may exacerbate cardiac arrhythmias. 43. Enalapril, after hydrolysis to enalaprilat, inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in humans and animals. 44. ACE catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, which also stimulates aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex. 45. Inhibition of ACE decreases plasma angiotensin II levels, leading to reduced vasopressor activity and decreased aldosterone secretion. 46. The reduction in aldosterone secretion is small but results in slight increases in serum potassium levels. 47. In hypertensive patients treated with enalapril alone for up to 48 weeks, mean increases in serum potassium of approximately 0.2 mEq/L were observed. 48. In patients treated with enalapril plus a thiazide diuretic, serum potassium levels remained essentially unchanged. 49. Removal of angiotensin II negative feedback on renin secretion leads to increased plasma renin activity. 50. ACE is identical to kininase, an enzyme that degrades bradykinin. 51. Whether increased bradykinin levels contribute to the therapeutic effects of enalapril remains unclear. 52. 53. Enalapril was antihypertensive in all racial groups studied, though black hypertensive patients may respond less favorably.
